content: The therapeutic courses of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) likely reduce the incidence of placental malaria infection. This conclusion is based on data from 59 observational studies, with a moderate level of certainty due to a clear dose-response gradient. There were no serious concerns regarding inconsistency, indirectness, or imprecision, but there was a serious risk of publication bias due to participation bias, as women who did not attend antenatal care (ANC) were likely different from those receiving three doses of intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp). The effect of SP on preterm delivery remains uncertain. Data from 46 observational studies suggest a very low certainty of evidence due to serious publication bias and inconsistency. The difference observed was 4 fewer preterm deliveries per 1,000, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 5 fewer to 3 fewer. Similarly, the impact of SP on stillbirths and/or abortions is uncertain. Data from 46 observational studies indicate a very low certainty of evidence due to serious inconsistency and indirectness. The difference observed was 3 fewer stillbirths per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 4 fewer to 2 fewer. Therapeutic courses of SP may result in little to no difference in maternal deaths. This conclusion is based on data from 6 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 8,755 participants. The difference observed was 1 more maternal death per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 2 fewer to 5 more. The certainty of evidence is low due to very few events and wide confidence intervals that include both no effect and an appreciable risk. SP likely improves mean birth weight. Data from 82 observational studies show a mean difference (MD) of 57 grams higher per dose of SP, with a 95% CI ranging from 44 grams higher to 69 grams higher. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to a clear dose-response gradient. SP may improve maternal hemoglobin levels. Data from 46 observational studies indicate a mean increase of 22 g/L per dose of SP, with a low certainty of evidence due to a clear dose-response gradient. Therapeutic courses of SP may increase maternal serious adverse events. This conclusion is based on data from 8 studies, with a low certainty of evidence due to a very serious risk of bias, as no events were reported in the comparison arm. SP likely increases maternal adverse events compared to placebo or case management. Data from 16 studies involving 8,122 participants suggest a moderate certainty of evidence due to serious imprecision. Perennial malaria chemoprevention (PMC), formerly known as intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi), likely reduces the incidence of clinical malaria. Data from 10,602 participants in 10 RCTs show a reduction of 220 fewer cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 280 fewer to 150 fewer. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. PMC with SP likely reduces the incidence of clinical malaria. Data from 8,774 participants in 8 RCTs show a reduction of 160 fewer cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 230 fewer to 90 fewer. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. PMC with artesunate-amodiaquine (AS-AQ) likely reduces the incidence of clinical malaria. Data from 547 participants in 1 RCT show a reduction of 330 fewer cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 520 fewer to 120 fewer. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. PMC with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-P) likely reduces the incidence of clinical malaria. Data from 147 participants in 1 RCT show a reduction of 3,720 fewer cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 430 fewer to 325 fewer. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. PMC with SP and artesunate (SP+AS) reduces the incidence of clinical malaria. Data from 508 participants in 1 RCT show a reduction of 290 fewer cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 510 fewer to 40 fewer. The certainty of evidence is high. PMC with SP may reduce the incidence of severe malaria. Data from 1,347 participants in 2 RCTs show a reduction of 1 fewer case per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 9 fewer to 11 more. The certainty of evidence is low due to serious inconsistency and imprecision. PMC with DHA-P may increase the incidence of severe malaria. Data from 147 participants in 1 RCT show an increase of 8 more cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 21 fewer to 144 more. The certainty of evidence is low due to very serious imprecision. PMC with AS-AQ likely reduces all-cause mortality slightly. Data from 684 participants in 1 RCT show an increase of 8 more deaths per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 15 fewer to 56 more. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. PMC with DHA-P may reduce all-cause mortality slightly. Data from 196 participants in 1 RCT show a reduction of 7 fewer deaths per 1,000, with a low certainty of evidence due to very serious imprecision. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) likely reduces the incidence of clinical malaria in children under 5 years. Data from 8 studies show a reduction of 315 fewer cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 335 fewer to 212 fewer. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious inconsistency. SMC with SP+AQ likely reduces the incidence of clinical malaria in children under 5 years. Data from 4 studies show a reduction of 338 fewer cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 374 fewer to 314 fewer. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious inconsistency. SMC with SP+AQ likely reduces the incidence of clinical malaria in children aged 5–9 years. Data from 1 study show a reduction of 248 fewer cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 292 fewer to 219 fewer. The certainty of evidence is high. SMC with AS-AQ may reduce the incidence of clinical malaria in children aged 6–15 years. Data from 1 study show a reduction of 64 fewer cases per 1,000, with a 95% CI ranging from 89 fewer to 47 fewer. The certainty of evidence is low due to very serious risk of bias.
